definition: Drametrics is a quantitative approach to analyzing dramatic texts that emerged as part of the broader field of computational criticism (distant reading) and digital humanities.
details: The term was introduced by Polish-American scholar and playwright, Magda Romanska in 2014 in her essay "Drametrics: What Dramaturgs Should Learn From Mathematicians" included in The Routledge Companion to Dramaturgy. In her foundational essay, Romanska traces how mathematics had been implicitly present in dramatic theory since the 19th century, citing Gustav Freytag's geometric patterns of dramatic structure in classic Greek tragedy as an early example of mathematical thinking applied to dramatic analysis. Based on this, Romanska proposed a transvergent theory of dramatic structure that combines classical Aristotelian dramatic theory with mathematical and computational methods to analyze theatrical works. Romanska posits that these mathematical relationships contribute to the aesthetic and dramatic effectiveness of theatrical works, just as the golden ratio (approximately 1.618:1) and Fibonacci spiral appear in classical architecture and visual art. Romanska shows not only that the drametrics theory works for the conventional well-made play, such as Henrik Ibsen’s A Doll’s House, but also for the more contemporary dramas such as Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot.

explainer.lead: Drametrics turns the structure of a play into something that can be measured: who shares a scene, who speaks, and how those patterns change. It gives researchers a way to compare plays and spot dramatic structures that ordinary close reading might miss.

tiers.eli5: Imagine drawing a map of a play, with a dot for each character and a line whenever two characters share a scene. The map can show who is at the center of the story, which characters form groups, and who is left out. Drametrics uses tables, counts, and computer analysis to make maps like this and study how plays are built.
tiers.practitioner: A typical workflow encodes a play in TEI-XML or VED, extracts speeches, stage directions, and character co-appearances, then applies network and statistical analysis. Katharsis can automate quantitative analysis and visualize character networks, while scene-detection methods can infer breaks from entrances, exits, and dialogue changes. Apparent mathematical regularities should not automatically be treated as evidence of the playwright's conscious design.
tiers.paperLevel: Drametrics is the quantitative and computational analysis of dramatic structure within computational criticism, distant reading, and digital humanities. A basic representation is a configuration matrix M, where M[s,c] records whether character c appears in scene s; co-appearances support analyses of centrality, clustering, isolation, and structural change. Magda Romanska introduced the term in her 2014 essay "Drametrics: What Dramaturgs Should Learn From Mathematicians," building on earlier mathematical poetics such as Solomon Marcus's configuration matrices; a central limit is that observed proportions or patterns may be coincidental rather than intentional.

explainer.example: For a Shakespeare play, make one row per scene and one column per character, marking each appearance. Turning shared scenes into a character network can reveal a central plot figure, a cluster that frequently interacts, and an isolated group; repeating the matrix over time shows how those configurations change.

usedIn.name: Katharsis
usedIn.detail: Processes TEI-XML drama texts to extract metadata and dialogue statistics and visualize character networks.

usedIn.name: Academic theatre research
usedIn.detail: Supports large-scale comparisons, structural analysis, and quantitative evidence for literary theories.

usedIn.name: Computational dramaturgy
usedIn.detail: Applies character mapping and structural analysis to playwriting, directing, criticism, and performance analysis.

usedIn.name: Digital interactive storytelling
usedIn.detail: Extends dramatic-structure analysis to video game narratives and hybrid physical-digital performance.

explainer.intuition: A play is not only a sequence of words; it is also a changing arrangement of characters, speeches, scenes, and themes. Encoding those arrangements makes it possible to measure relationships and compare structures across scenes or entire bodies of drama.
howItWorks: Encode the play's speeches, stage directions, characters, and structural divisions.
Build configuration matrices recording which characters appear together in each scene.
Measure dialogue distribution, network density, centrality, clustering, and other structural patterns.
Use character changes, dialogue shifts, and thematic transitions to detect dramatic units and scene boundaries.
Visualize and compare the results, optionally adding topic, sentiment, or linguistic analysis.
explainer.whyItMatters: Drametrics can expose patterns hidden from scene-by-scene close reading and provide quantitative evidence for arguments about dramatic form. It also makes comparisons across many plays practical and connects theatre studies with computational and digital-humanities methods.
misconceptions: Finding a mathematical pattern does not prove that the playwright designed it deliberately.
Quantitative analysis complements close reading rather than making interpretation unnecessary.
The approach is not limited to conventional well-made plays; Romanska also applied it to Waiting for Godot.

diagram.caption: Drametrics converts an encoded play into structural data, then analyzes that data to reveal dramatic patterns.
